extracted.intended_audience: scholars, students, and researchers interested in the sociology of humor and jokes
extracted.subtask_description: Bibliographic/preview page for an academic book analyzing jokes as a genre and their relationship to social background, taste, and cultural differences. The book uses interviews, survey data, and historical materials to study how jokes are evaluated across groups and nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appreciation and evaluation of jokes by different social groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers the appreciation and evaluation of jokes by different social groups and in different cultures, and its relationship with wider humor styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book explores how various social groups appraise jokes (some calling jokes 'their favorite kind [of] humor', others 'completely devoid of humor' or 'a form of intellectual poverty').

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between humor and social background (gender, age, region, class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examines the relationship between humor and gender, age, regional background, and especially social class in the Netherlands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses a combination of interview materials, survey data, and historical materials to explore how social background shapes sense of humor and joke appreciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Status/prestige of the joke genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates the social status of the joke as a genre — noted as 'not a very prestigious genre' and of particularly low status in the Netherlands compared to the US.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book treats the joke's lack of status as a central analytic entry point for questions about humor and taste, tracing its decline in status from the sixteenth century onward.

rubrics_metrics.name: History and change of topics and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Describes the history of the joke genre and the way the topics and the tone of jokes have changed over the last fifty years of the twentieth century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical materials are used to document topical and tonal shifts in jokes over time and their implications for taste and acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: National differences in sense of humor (American vs Dutch)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzes national differences, specifically exploring differences between the American and the Dutch sense of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparisons are drawn using interview and survey materials to illustrate cross-national variation in joke appreciation and style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke telling as communication style
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers joke telling itself as a communication style and social practice (explicitly listed as a chapter topic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigates the role of joke telling in interaction, including how people tell jokes, contexts for telling, and communicative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensiveness and boundary transgression (sexual, ethnic, hurtful jokes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Addresses offensive and hurtful forms of joking, including sexual jokes, ethnic jokes, and boundary transgression as dimensions of joke evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explores objections and moral reactions to jokes and how offensiveness affects appreciation across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lowbrow versus intellectual/esthetic distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Explores distinctions between lowbrow/popular humor and intellectual/esthetic humor, including evaluative language like 'intellectual' and 'esthetic' versus 'vulgar' or 'coarse'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents how class and education shape judgments about what counts as 'good' versus 'bad' taste in humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joke repertoire, tellers, and role of performers
rubrics_metrics.description: Considers the repertoire of jokes people know and tell, the characteristics of joke tellers, and the role of performers (comedians, cabaret artists, television programs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes discussion of joke books, joke culture, and the social role of joke-telling individuals and media contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique and effect (punch line, shock effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attends to technical aspects of jokes such as punch lines and shock effects as contributors to perceived funniness or offensiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyzes how formal features and shock strategies function in joke delivery and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological triangulation (interviews, surveys, historical materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employs a mixed-methods approach combining interview materials, survey data, and historical materials to study jokes sociologically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book's conclusions are grounded in multiple data sources to connect qualitative impressions with quantitative patterns and historical change.
